name: New Jersey
summary_text: A trans visitor to New Jersey is bound first by United States federal rules, which apply identically in every state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are decided only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker stay valid until expiry, but travellers whose papers no longer match their presentation can expect questions at issuance and at the border. The ACLU's lawsuit on behalf of seven plaintiffs and Lambda Legal's documentation guidance are the outstanding points of challenge, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue its changed treatment of trans passports.  Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, followed by the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, requires refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement treats a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth as potential fraud, carrying a permanent bar. A visitor travelling for sport should assume the rule is applied mechanically.  Checkpoint procedures risk involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as steps that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.  Inside New Jersey the measured legal environment is among the most protective in the country. The July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places New Jersey in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier whose laws have, in the assessment's words, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. On the separate state-by-state dataset of killings of trans women covering 2008 to 2025, New Jersey records 3.4 per 100,000 per year, four recorded deaths in total, and is labelled 'Safest States'.

name: New Mexico
summary_text: New Mexico stands under the national framework of the United States, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.  Entry and screening follow national rules regardless of which state the visitor lands in. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide, which sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.  Facility use and identity documents are regulated state by state, so the rules encountered inside New Mexico differ from those in states that restrict them. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances in some jurisdictions, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at a state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following. Multiple foreign governments, at least eight European countries including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens after the federal document and data rules, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies four states now designated do-not-travel for trans people.  Within that national picture, New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The ranking is built from a rubric applied over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, and it records that the laws of the protective-tier states have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.  New Mexico also operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the home state of the person travelling for it. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state with a care ban, and it applies alongside, not instead of, the federal document and entry rules.

sources.title: HB7 - Gender-Affirming Care, Abortion and Sexual Orientation Protections Act (2023)
sources.documents: Legally codifies, protects and defends gender affirming care, abortion, sexual orientation protections and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for interstate travellers; basis for 'sanctuary state' status for transgender youths
sources.detail: Formally passed New Mexico Legislature March 2023 and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham; no URL visible in article text

sources.title: 2019 Birth Certificate / Driver's License Gender Designation Law - repeal of 1984 surgery requirement
sources.documents: Allows transgender people to change legal gender to male, female or neutral 'X' on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs without sex reassignment surgery; establishes forms and parental consent rule for minors

sources.title: An Act Relating to Human Rights - New Mexico anti-discrimination law
sources.documents: Bans unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership; later amendments remove 15-employee exemption and explicitly include local entities/counties/schools/universities
sources.detail: Effective July 1, 2003; 2019 repeal bill passed 59-0 House 36-0 Senate signed by Gov. Lujan Grisham effective July 1, 2019; March 2023 loophole-closure bill signed with emergency clause; 1985 Gov. Toney Anaya executive order on public employment cited as predecessor; no URL visible
